newsitem.title: USA: Jurors told drug benefits outweigh FDA process.
newsitem.headline: Jurors told drug benefits outweigh FDA process.

text.p: Lawyers for a doctor accused of illegally dispensing an experimental cancer drug asked jurors Friday to consider whether federal procedures for approving new drugs outweigh his attempts to save lives.

In closing arguments capping a two-month criminal trial, attorneys for doctor Stanislaw Burzynski said federal regulators were aware he was treating cancer and AIDS patients with the unapproved drug antineoplaston for more than a decade before seeking an indictment to shut down his practice.
"You are going to decide really how far government gets to go. That's really what's involved in this case," said Rick Jaffe, who represents Burzynski and the Burzynski Research Institute.

Burzynski, 54, was charged in a 75-count indictment with criminal contempt of a court order, violating federal drug laws and defrauding insurance companies by prescribing antineoplaston, a synthetic drug derived from peptides in human blood and urine, to patients across the country.

The Polish-born Burzynski was ordered in 1983 to stop shipping the experimental drug out of state in violation of Food and Drug Administration regulations. Federal prosecutors said he ignored the order and continued operating a medical practice and drug manufacturing facility that netted $40 million a year from patients and insurance companies.

To get around the court's order that he not ship the drug out of state, Burzynski had his patients -- many terminally ill cancer victims turning to him out of desperation -- come to Texas for treatments and antineoplaston prescriptions.

"They come, they stay for 10 days, two weeks, they leave, they take the medicine with them," said Assistant U.S. Attorney George Tallichet, who called the arrangement "an unbelievable pattern of wilful contempt" of the court order.

The case attracted national attention as a trial not only of Burzynski but of the FDA's process of approving new drugs that terminally ill patients said takes too long and restricts access to experimental treatments.
The seven-woman, five-man jury was expected to begin deliberations in the case late Friday afternoon.
